summary: Describes evaluation test cases for congestion control of interactive real-time media over wireless networks, where capacity and delay can change quickly. It supports testing RTP-based congestion control for a good user experience. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Wi-Fi and phone networks change speed all the time. This document lists tricky practice situations to test whether video-call software can keep up when the wireless link gets better and worse.

subtitle: Test scenarios for real-time media congestion control over cellular and Wi-Fi networks

tldr.problem: Wireless networks (cellular and Wi-Fi) have very different characteristics from wired networks—capacity changes rapidly, handovers cause packet bursts, and queuing behavior is unique—so congestion control algorithms must be tested specifically for wireless environments.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8869 defines test cases for evaluating RTP-based congestion control algorithms over LTE/5G cellular networks and Wi-Fi, modeling variable load, bad radio coverage, and the specific challenges of wireless links.
tldr.outcome: These wireless-specific test cases complement RFC 8867's core tests, ensuring algorithms work well on mobile networks where conditions change much faster than on fixed wired networks.

today: RFC 8869 is an Informational document published in January 2021 and provides the primary framework for testing congestion control algorithms on wireless networks. It is used by mobile network vendors, device manufacturers, and researchers developing real-time communication solutions for cellular and Wi-Fi environments.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Wireless networks present challenges that wired networks do not. In cellular networks, the base station maintains individual queues per radio bearer per user, creating different queuing dynamics than shared wired bottlenecks where all traffic competes in a single queue. User mobility, handovers between cells, and the dynamic nature of radio link adaptation cause rapid and unpredictable bandwidth changes. Wi-Fi networks have their own challenges with shared medium access and variable coverage areas.

RFC 8867 provides core test cases for congestion control algorithms in a general sense. However, the unique characteristics of wireless networks—variable link capacity that can change in milliseconds, handover events that cause packet loss bursts, location-dependent signal strength, and different queue management from cellular base stations—require additional test scenarios. RFC 8869 extends the evaluation framework specifically for wireless access networks, building on the evaluation guidelines in RFC 8868.
sections.plainLanguage: Video calls over phone networks and Wi-Fi are trickier than over regular Internet cables. The speed changes super fast, connections sometimes drop and reconnect, and the way traffic gets queued is completely different. So you need special tests to check if an algorithm works for mobile.

sections.title: Cellular Network Test Scenarios
sections.content:
Cellular networks have unique properties that distinguish them from wired networks. Each user has per-radio-bearer queues at the base station, users can experience both inter- and intra-Radio Access Technology (RAT) handovers that cause temporary packet loss or queueing, and the network scheduler can vary link capacity as fast as every millisecond based on radio conditions, distance from the base station, interference, and other users' activity. Users may reach the cell edge, causing signal degradation and retransmissions.

RFC 8869 defines two primary cellular test scenarios: (1) Varying Network Load, which tests performance as the number of users in the cell changes over time using a Poisson arrival model to keep load stable, and (2) Bad Radio Coverage, which tests performance when users experience poor signal conditions with higher error rates and longer delays. Both tests use a simulator (such as the LTE simulator in NS-3) rather than live networks because live cellular networks cannot be controlled reliably for repeatable testing. The test setup includes multi-cell deployments with mobility models, configurable AQM settings, and specific downlink and uplink user intensities.
sections.plainLanguage: On cellular networks, the speed changes not just because of congestion but also because you move around, other people start using the network, the signal gets weaker, and your phone switches between base stations. The tests measure whether an algorithm handles all these real mobile situations.

sections.title: Wi-Fi Network Test Scenarios
sections.content:
Wi-Fi networks present different challenges than cellular. In Wi-Fi, multiple devices share a common medium using contention-based access (CSMA/CA), so all devices on an access point share the same bottleneck. Link capacity depends on distance from the router, interference from other wireless devices, and the negotiated data rate, which adapts automatically based on signal quality. Wi-Fi implementations may use different queue management schemes and support features like Enhanced Distributed Channel Access (EDCA) for prioritization.

RFC 8869 addresses Wi-Fi test scenarios involving bottlenecks at different points: either at the wired backhaul (between the Wi-Fi network and Internet core), or at the Wi-Fi access network itself (between the device and router). These tests examine behavior under typical Wi-Fi conditions where heterogeneous link rates occur (some devices further from the router, hence slower), and where EDCA/WMM Quality of Service mechanisms may be active. The test framework allows evaluation of how well algorithms adapt to the specific characteristics of Wi-Fi, where capacity can vary dramatically based on physical location and interference.
sections.plainLanguage: Wi-Fi is shared among everyone in range, like a shared hallway versus your own cable line. Your speed depends on how far you are from the router and how many neighbors are using Wi-Fi too. Tests check if algorithms work when you move around the house or when other people start downloading.

sections.title: Test Configuration and Metrics
sections.content:
The cellular test configuration specifies detailed simulation parameters: 3GPP case 1 propagation model, MIMO antenna patterns, mobility speeds of 3 to 30 km/h, 10 MHz transmission bandwidth in a multi-cell deployment (21 cells), a proportional fair scheduler with no priority, and either on or off Active Queue Management. Round-trip time is 40 to 150 ms, user arrivals follow a Poisson distribution, and simulation duration is 91 seconds with an evaluation period from 30 to 60 seconds (excluding warm-up). Media sources follow RFC 8867's definitions for VBR video and CBR audio.

Both cellular and Wi-Fi tests measure the same classes of metrics as RFC 8867: flow-level metrics (end-to-end delay, bitrate variation, packet loss, convergence time) and transport-level metrics (bandwidth utilization, queue length). The key difference is that wireless tests exercise the algorithm under more dynamic conditions—rapidly changing capacity, handovers, and signal-dependent variations—to ensure robust performance in real mobile deployments. Tests can run with or without specific active queue management schemes to capture behavior across different network configurations.
sections.plainLanguage: The tests set up realistic cellular and Wi-Fi networks in a simulator with moving phones, other users arriving and leaving, and signal strength that changes. Engineers measure whether video quality stays smooth, how much data the algorithm wastes or saves, and how fast it adapts to changes.

sections.title: Wireless-Specific Challenges
sections.content:
Wireless networks differ from wired networks in how congestion arises and how it manifests. In wired networks, congestion is primarily due to aggregate traffic exceeding link capacity, causing packet loss and queuing delay. In wireless networks, congestion interacts with radio link quality—poor signal causes bit errors and retransmissions, which consume bandwidth even when network load is moderate. Handovers between cells or between radio access technologies (like switching from LTE to 5G) cause brief service interruptions and can generate bursts of queued packets once the new connection is established.

These wireless-specific factors require algorithms to be evaluated against scenarios that do not exist in pure wired networks. RFC 8869 recommends using simulation over live networks for repeatable, controlled testing of these scenarios. The guidelines complement RFC 8867's core scenarios and RFC 8868's evaluation framework, collectively providing a complete methodology for assessing real-time media congestion control across the full range of network environments—from fixed high-speed Internet to variable-capacity mobile access.
sections.plainLanguage: Radio links are unpredictable in ways cables are not. Bad signal makes the network slow even if nobody else is using it. Switching between networks causes hiccups. Good algorithms need to handle all these mobile-only problems, and the tests make sure they do.
